findings.evidence: Synthetic cases are labelled as the baseline: "baseline_engine": "clef-flash (synthetic)", "baseline_role": expected_role (a hand-written label from test_benchmarks). Transcript cases (lines 169-170) use "transcript (real)" with baseline_role set by a keyword heuristic, not a clef-flash output. Yet the report at lines 225-226, 232 and 306-307 is headed 'clef-flash' and prints 'Top-1 Agreement (Kev-4B vs clef-flash)'.
findings.suggested_investigation: Run the script with --source transcripts and inspect the case dicts (--export to a temp dir) to confirm baseline_engine is not clef-flash. Then check that the summary header and metric labels name the actual baseline source per case.
findings.why_it_matters: The printed agreement numbers claim to measure agreement with clef-flash, but for the default --source transcripts run (line 198/197) the 'baseline' is a keyword guess. A reader could take the metric as evidence that a model matches the production router when it only matches the heuristic.

findings.evidence: "baseline_latency_ms": 160.0 is hardcoded for synthetic cases (line 125), and the transcript path does the same (line 173). Line 301 averages these into avg_base_lat, and lines 310-312 print "Kev-0.8B Speedup over clef-flash: {speedup:.1f}x faster" from avg_base_lat / avg_08b_lat.
findings.suggested_investigation: Check whether any case in the run carries a measured latency_ms (ledger source, lines 97 and 173). Compute the speedup only over cases with a measured baseline latency, and omit the line when there are none.
findings.why_it_matters: The speedup figure divides a measured 0.8B latency by a constant 160 ms that was never measured for the baseline. For transcript and synthetic cases the 'clef-flash' latency is invented, so the speedup claim has no measured basis. The wording 'x faster' is also misleading when the ratio is below 1.

findings.evidence: expected_role = "code" if any(w in p_lower for w in ["fix", "implement", "tweak", "replace", "add"]) else "review"
findings.suggested_investigation: Count how many transcript prompts that contain 'address' or 'prefix' get role 'code'. Switch to word-boundary matching (for example a regex with \b) and compare the agreement numbers before and after.
findings.why_it_matters: The keyword test is a raw substring match on the lowercased prompt, so 'add' matches 'address', 'padding', and 'ladder', and 'fix' matches 'prefix' and 'suffix'. Mislabelled baseline roles shift the agreement percentages (lines 297-298) for the default transcript source. The labels are inputs to the metric, so this affects the result.

findings.evidence: except Exception as e: elapsed_ms = ...; return None, elapsed_ms. Then lines 274-275 call parse_answer(...) when res is None, which returns ("unknown", 0.0, 1.0), and lines 297-298 count every zip pair, including 'unknown', against total = len(cases).
findings.suggested_investigation: Run with KEV_4B_URL pointed at a closed port and check the summary line for Kev-4B vs clef-flash. Then decide whether to exclude unavailable cases from the denominator and report a separate availability count.
findings.why_it_matters: An endpoint that is down, times out, or returns a non-JSON body is recorded as a role disagreement rather than excluded. The top-1 percentages therefore fall with endpoint availability, not with model quality. The run still exits 0 with all rows showing OFF, so an operator can misread the summary.

findings.evidence: When the live call fails, the code loads .claude/kev_4b_benchmark.json and sets res_4b = {"answers": {"role": c_entry}}, lat_4b = c_entry.get("latency_ms", 185.0). Lines 288 and 291 then print lat_4b as the live '4B ms' value, and line 282 adds it to kev4b_lats.
findings.suggested_investigation: Run with the 4B endpoint down and a cache file present. Check whether the table and the mean latency distinguish cached rows. Add a source marker per row or keep cached rows out of the live latency list.
findings.why_it_matters: Cached benchmark answers and latencies from an earlier run are shown and averaged as if they were live results. The 'Kev-4B' column and the 'Mean Latency' figure can therefore reflect stale data with no marker, and the fallback default of 185.0 is also an unmeasured constant.

findings.evidence: "baseline_role": rec.get("decision") or rec.get("clef_output", {}).get("role"), and the same pattern on lines 95-96. These run outside the try at lines 81-84. A record with "clef_output": null, or a non-dict clef_output, raises AttributeError.
findings.suggested_investigation: Check the ledger for CLEF_ROUTE lines where clef_output is null or missing and decision is empty. Confirm whether the crash reproduces, then guard the field access with an isinstance check.
findings.why_it_matters: One malformed CLEF_ROUTE record in master_ledger.jsonl aborts extract_evaluation_cases, and main() does not catch it, so the whole --source ledger/both run crashes. Whether such records exist depends on the ledger, which I did not read.

findings.evidence: for t in brain_transcripts: try: ... for line in f: rec = json.loads(line) ... content = rec.get("content", "").strip() ... except Exception: pass (lines 178-179)
findings.suggested_investigation: Log the file path and exception in the except block, and move the try inside the per-line loop so one bad line does not drop the rest of the file. Compare the case count before and after on the same transcripts.
findings.why_it_matters: The broad except inside the per-file loop discards the rest of a transcript file on the first malformed line or non-string content. Extraction then silently returns fewer cases with no warning. This hides data loss and makes the case count hard to interpret.

findings.evidence: # Strict PII redaction / p = re.sub(r"[\w\.-]+@[\w\.-]+\.\w+", "[EMAIL]", p) / p = re.sub(r"password[:\s=]+[^\s]+", "[REDACTED]", p, flags=re.I)
findings.suggested_investigation: Confirm which secret-like strings appear in exported transcript cases. Either narrow the comment to what is redacted or extend the redaction. Decide whether --export should be restricted to a known directory.
findings.why_it_matters: The comment says 'Strict PII redaction', but only email addresses and 'password' assignments are scrubbed. Tokens, API keys, and other secrets in user prompts are not redacted. With --export (lines 213-218) those prompts are written to an arbitrary file path.

notes: Single-file packet, reviewed from the whole-file content in the packet; no tool calls used. The script only sends prompts to loopback ports by default (lines 24-25). If KEV_4B_URL or KEV_08B_URL is overridden to a remote host, transcript prompts would leave the machine; this is configuration-dependent and not reported as a finding. Line 107 hardcodes a GameAddr (0x005bda40) inside a benchmark prompt string. It is not used as code or an allowlist entry, so I did not flag it. I did not read .claude/master_ledger.jsonl or .claude/kev_4b_benchmark.json (outside the packet), so f6 and the cache-format assumptions in f5 are unverified. No gate or test is affected: this is a benchmark script, not a gate, so the exit-code concern does not apply.
